title: Angle Relationships Grade 6: Solve for the Missing Angle + Free Quiz
meta_title: Angle Relationships Grade 6: Find Missing Angles
meta_desc: Master angle relationships in Grade 6: complementary, supplementary, adjacent, linear pairs and vertical angles, and solve for a missing angle. Free quiz.
excerpt: Once a Grade 6 student sees that two angles on a straight line always add to 180°, half the geometry homework solves itself. Here is how to turn each angle relationship into a one-line equation, plus a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 6 student a diagram where two angles sit on a straight line, one marked 130° and the other marked x, and watch what happens. Half the class reaches for a protractor. The other half — the ones who have grasped angle relationships in Grade 6 — just write x + 130° = 180° and are done in five seconds. That gap is the whole point of this topic. It is not really about measuring angles; it is about recognising a relationship and turning it into a short equation you can solve.

There are only five relationships worth memorising at this level, and each one gives you exactly one rule. Learn the rule, write the equation, solve for the missing angle. In my experience tutoring students in Class 6, the ones who struggle are almost never weak at the arithmetic — they simply have not learned to name which relationship the picture is showing. So let us fix that first.

The five angle relationships every Grade 6 student needs

Here is the entire toolkit. Notice how each row is really just a number (90 or 180) or a copy rule — that is all an angle relationship is.

RelationshipWhat it meansThe rule
Complementary anglesTwo angles that together form a right angleSum = 90°
Supplementary anglesTwo angles that together form a straight lineSum = 180°
Adjacent anglesTwo angles sharing a vertex and one arm, side by sideThey just add up
Linear pairAdjacent angles whose outer arms make a straight lineSum = 180°
Vertically opposite anglesThe angles across from each other when two lines crossThey are equal

A quick way to keep 90 and 180 straight

Students mix up complementary and supplementary constantly. The trick I give them: C comes before S in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180. Complementary is the smaller one (90°), supplementary is the bigger one (180°). One student told me she remembers ‘complementary corners’ because a corner is a right angle. Whatever sticks, use it.

Turning a relationship into an equation

This is the skill the whole chapter is building towards. Every problem follows the same three steps, so the routine matters more than any single question.

  • Step 1 — name it. Look at the diagram. Are the two angles on a straight line? Do they share a vertex? Do two lines cross? Name the relationship out loud.
  • Step 2 — write the rule as an equation. Straight line means the two angles sum to 180°. A right angle means they sum to 90°. Crossing lines mean the opposite angles are equal.
  • Step 3 — solve for the missing angle. Substitute the known number and subtract, or isolate x.

Worked example: supplementary angles

Two angles form a linear pair. One is 115°, the other is x. Because they lie on a straight line, they are supplementary, so x + 115° = 180°. Subtract: x = 180° − 115° = 65°. That is it — no protractor, no guessing.

Worked example: an equation with a variable on both sides

Sometimes the two angles are given as expressions. Say two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x + 10)° and 50°. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so 2x + 10 = 50. Subtract 10 from both sides to get 2x = 40, then divide by 2: x = 20. This is where angle relationships quietly turn into early algebra practice, which is exactly why NCERT places the topic where it does.

The mistakes I see most often

Two errors show up again and again, and both are easy to prevent.

First: students assume any two angles that look next to each other must add to 180°. They do not — only a genuine linear pair (outer arms forming a straight line) does. If the outer arms bend, the angles are just adjacent and you can only add them, not set them to 180°.

Second: after solving, students forget to answer the actual question. If a problem asks for the larger of two supplementary angles and you found x = 40°, the answer might be the other angle, 140°. Always re-read what was asked. This one honest habit — checking what the question wanted — saves more marks than any formula.

A short practice routine that works

Ten minutes, three times a week, beats a marathon session the night before a test. A pattern that works well: on the first day, name relationships from diagrams without solving anything — pure recognition. On the second day, solve for a missing angle using plain numbers. On the third, mix in one or two questions with a variable like 3x − 5. The variety forces the student to choose the rule rather than repeat the last one, and choosing is where fluency lives.

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering all five angle relationships and the solve-for-x skill. Let your child attempt it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 6 Angle Relationships Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on complementary, supplementary, adjacent, linear pair and vertically opposite angles, including solving for a missing angle. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 angle relationships and missing angles

questions.q: Two angles are complementary. If one is 35°, what is the other?
Two angles form a linear pair. One measures 118°. Find the other.
questions.explanation: A linear pair lies on a straight line, so the angles are supplementary: 180° − 118° = 62°.

questions.q: Two lines cross. One angle is 74°. What is the angle vertically opposite it?
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are always equal, so it is 74°.

questions.q: Which pair of angles must add up to 180°?
questions.explanation: Supplementary angles sum to 180°. Complementary angles sum to 90°.

questions.q: Two vertically opposite angles are (2x + 10)° and 50°. Find x.
questions.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal: 2x + 10 = 50, so 2x = 40 and x = 20.

questions.q: An angle and its complement are equal. What is each angle?
questions.explanation: If both are equal and add to 90°, each is 90° ÷ 2 = 45°.

questions.q: Angles of 3x° and 60° together form a right angle. Find x.
questions.explanation: A right angle is 90°, so 3x + 60 = 90, giving 3x = 30 and x = 10.

faq.q: What are the five angle relationships taught in Grade 6?
faq.a: Complementary angles (sum 90°), supplementary angles (sum 180°), adjacent angles (side by side, sharing an arm), linear pairs (adjacent angles on a straight line, sum 180°) and vertically opposite angles (equal, formed when two lines cross).

faq.q: How do I find a missing angle using an angle relationship?
faq.a: Name the relationship, write its rule as an equation, then solve. For example, if x and 120° are supplementary, write x + 120° = 180° and subtract to get x = 60°.

faq.q: What is the difference between complementary and supplementary angles?
faq.a: Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°. A memory hook: C comes before S, and 90 comes before 180.

faq.q: Are a linear pair and supplementary angles the same thing?
faq.a: Every linear pair is supplementary, but not every supplementary pair is a linear pair. A linear pair must also be adjacent, with the outer arms forming one straight line. Supplementary angles just need to total 180°, even if they are drawn apart.
